questions.prompt: A dedicated SQL Server box has 64 GB of RAM and `max server memory` has been left at its out-of-box default. What is likely to happen, and why?
options: The buffer pool is capped at 4 GB regardless of max server memory, so the extra RAM simply goes unused
Nothing — SQL Server automatically reserves a safe margin for the OS even at the default setting
The Database Engine will keep consuming RAM up to the OS limit, potentially starving the OS and any other services on the box, because the default is effectively unlimited
SQL Server refuses to start until max server memory is set explicitly
questions.explain: max server memory ships effectively unlimited. Left at that default, the Database Engine will happily take memory the OS or any co-hosted services need, and the server can start paging — exactly the real-world mistake Lesson 3 warns a DBA to avoid by setting it explicitly.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ is the background process that writes all current dirty pages from the buffer pool to disk, shortening how much transaction log SQL Server must replay during crash recovery — but it does not, by itself, free buffer pool memory.
questions.explain: Checkpoint keeps the data files current for recovery purposes by flushing dirty pages, but it's the lazy writer, not checkpoint, that actually frees buffer pool memory by evicting unused pages — the two background processes have distinct jobs even though both touch the buffer pool.

questions.prompt: Match each system database to what it actually does, per Lesson 6.
right: Instance-level metadata — logins, linked servers, and the list of every other database and where its files live
Hidden, read-only database holding every system object; lets a version upgrade replace it cleanly without touching master or user databases
The literal template SQL Server copies when CREATE DATABASE runs; any object or setting change here applies to every future database
Where Agent stores job definitions, schedules, and history, along with backup/restore history
questions.explain: master holds instance-level metadata including the list of every database and its files. resourcedb is hidden and read-only, holding system objects separately so upgrades can replace it cleanly. model is the literal template copied for every CREATE DATABASE. msdb holds Agent's job definitions and history plus backup/restore history.

questions.prompt: `sys.dm_os_wait_stats` shows `SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD` as one of the top wait types on a server. What does that suggest is happening, and at what level?
options: A deadlock between two transactions waiting on each other's locks
CPU pressure at the SQLOS scheduling layer — tasks are running long enough between voluntary yields that others are queuing behind them on the same scheduler
Disk I/O pressure — pages aren't being read into the buffer pool fast enough
A memory grant spilling to tempdb because of a bad row-count estimate
questions.explain: SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD is recorded when a task voluntarily yields its scheduler turn. A high volume of it points to CPU pressure at the SQLOS scheduling layer itself — tasks running long enough between yields that others queue up — not a query-logic problem, a deadlock, or an I/O issue.

questions.prompt: What is a group Managed Service Account (gMSA), and why is it the current best practice for a SQL Server service account on a domain?
options: A SQL Server login whose password policy is enforced by CHECK_POLICY = ON
A shared built-in account, like Local System, used by every SQL Server service on a machine at once
A domain account type whose password is generated and rotated automatically by Active Directory, while still functioning as a normal, least-privilege, individually-auditable identity
A temporary account that expires automatically after 90 days and must be manually recreated
An account that only exists inside SQL Server itself, with no corresponding Active Directory object
An account type reserved exclusively for the sa login
questions.explain: A gMSA is a special AD account type whose password is generated and rotated automatically by Active Directory itself, while still functioning as a normal, least-privilege, individually-auditable domain identity. It removes the password-rotation operational burden a plain dedicated domain account carries, without giving up any least-privilege benefit.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes Local System or a similarly shared built-in account — exactly the anti-pattern Lesson 13 warns against: one shared identity across every service, with no individual accountability. A gMSA is the opposite — one dedicated, individually-auditable identity per service, with AD handling password rotation automatically instead of a human managing a shared credential.

questions.prompt: A stored procedure in `InventoryDB` creates a `#temp` table and joins it back against a column in `InventoryDB` itself. The query fails with a collation conflict error, even though nobody explicitly set an unusual collation anywhere. What's the most likely cause?
options: Temp tables can never be joined against permanent tables, regardless of collation
The stored procedure's owner has a different collation than the table's owner
SUBSTRING() silently changes a column's collation when used inside a temp table join
tempdb always uses the instance's default collation for object definitions, and that default differs from InventoryDB's own collation
questions.explain: tempdb always uses the instance's default collation for object definitions, regardless of any individual user database's collation. If InventoryDB's collation differs from the instance default, comparing a #temp table column against an InventoryDB column is ambiguous and SQL Server raises a collation conflict — the standard fix is an explicit COLLATE clause.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: `cost threshold for parallelism`'s out-of-box default is ________ — an optimizer-cost value set in the early 1990s that's far too low for modern hardware, which is why common practice raises it to somewhere in the 25-50 range.
questions.explain: The out-of-box default of 5 was set for hardware nothing like today's, causing small, cheap queries to go parallel unnecessarily. Raising it into the 25-50 range and tuning from observed workload behavior is common practice.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about post-install SQL Server configuration, per Lesson 9.
options: Out of the box, max server memory is effectively unlimited, so the Database Engine will consume RAM until the OS is starved
The out-of-box MAXDOP default of 0 lets a single query use every core, which can let one reporting query starve concurrent OLTP work
The out-of-box cost threshold for parallelism default of 5 is well-suited to modern hardware and rarely needs adjustment
Turning on backup compression makes backups smaller and, counter-intuitively, is often faster to write despite using more CPU
sp_configure changes always take effect immediately with no RECONFIGURE required
questions.explain: max server memory and MAXDOP both ship with defaults that can cause real problems — unlimited memory consumption and unrestricted query parallelism. Backup compression is a genuine win: smaller, often faster-to-write backups at the cost of some CPU. Cost threshold for parallelism's default of 5 is explicitly described as far too low for modern hardware, not well-suited to it. And sp_configure changes require RECONFIGURE to apply, with some options needing a restart besides.

questions.prompt: Put these screens of the SQL Server Setup wizard (`setup.exe`) in the order they actually appear, per Lesson 8.
items: Feature Selection — choose which components to install (Database Engine, Replication, Full-Text Search, etc.)
Instance Configuration — choose a default instance or a named instance
Server Configuration — enter service accounts and startup types for each service
Database Engine Configuration (Authentication Mode) — choose Windows Authentication or Mixed Mode
Database Engine Configuration (Data Directories) — set the default paths for data, log, and tempdb files
Collation — confirm or change the server-level default collation
questions.explain: Setup runs in a fixed order: Feature Selection, then Instance Configuration, then Server Configuration for service accounts, then the Database Engine Configuration screens for authentication mode and data directories, and finally Collation as the last convenient point to get it right before Install runs.

questions.prompt: A database is in SIMPLE recovery model and the server crashes at 2:15 PM. The last full backup ran at midnight. What's the most recent point this database can be recovered to?
options: Midnight — SIMPLE recovery has no log backups and therefore no point-in-time recovery; you can only restore to the last full or differential backup
2:15 PM — SIMPLE recovery can replay the active transaction log up to the moment of the crash
2:00 PM — SQL Server automatically takes an implicit log backup once per hour even in SIMPLE recovery
There is no recoverable point at all once a database in SIMPLE recovery crashes
questions.explain: SIMPLE recovery auto-truncates the log after every checkpoint, so there's no log backup chain and no point-in-time recovery — you can only restore to the point of the last full or differential backup, which here is midnight. Everything since then is gone.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the database options covered in Lesson 16.
options: AUTO_SHRINK sounds like good housekeeping, but it causes real index fragmentation and the file often just grows right back on the next load
AUTO_CLOSE is a good choice for a busy, constantly-connected production database because it keeps resources trimmed
READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON switches READ COMMITTED to use row versioning, so readers no longer block behind a writer's locks
PAGE_VERIFY CHECKSUM is the legacy option, superseded by TORN_PAGE_DETECTION as the modern default
Turning on READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT requires no other active connections in the database at the moment it's set
questions.explain: AUTO_SHRINK is a real anti-pattern — it fragments indexes and the space often gets reused immediately anyway. AUTO_CLOSE fights connection pooling and is wrong for a busy server with constant connections, not a good fit. READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT genuinely eliminates reader/writer blocking through row versioning, and setting it requires WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE with no other active connections. CHECKSUM has been the default since SQL Server 2005; TORN_PAGE_DETECTION is the older, weaker legacy option, not the other way around.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every database has exactly one ________ filegroup, which always contains the primary data file (.mdf) and the system catalog.
questions.explain: The PRIMARY filegroup is mandatory and always holds the .mdf and the system catalog. Unless told otherwise, every table and index also lands here by default; user-defined filegroups are additional, optional containers.

questions.prompt: Match each recovery model (or recovery concept) to what it actually does, per Lesson 17.
right: The log auto-truncates after every checkpoint; no log backups exist and there is no point-in-time recovery
The log retains every transaction until a log backup runs; this is what makes point-in-time recovery possible
Behaves like FULL for ordinary transactions but minimally logs certain bulk operations, at the cost of losing point-in-time restore through that window
Restoring a database to an exact moment using a chain of full, differential, and log backups
questions.explain: SIMPLE auto-truncates the log with no point-in-time recovery possible. FULL retains the log until a backup runs, which is exactly what enables point-in-time recovery. BULK_LOGGED behaves like FULL but minimally logs certain bulk operations, losing point-in-time restore through that specific window. Point-in-time recovery itself is restoring to an exact moment using the full/differential/log backup chain FULL recovery provides.

questions.prompt: If you run `CREATE DATABASE Reporting;` with no other clauses, where do the resulting data and log files land, and what determines their initial size?
options: SQL Server refuses to run CREATE DATABASE without an explicit ON PRIMARY clause
They land in whatever directory the current session's working directory happens to be
They land at the instance's default data/log directories, and SQL Server fills in every omitted detail — including initial size — by copying the model system database
The files are created with a 0 MB initial size and grow entirely on first use
questions.explain: The minimal CREATE DATABASE form is legal: SQL Server fills in every omitted piece from the model system database and the instance's default data/log paths. That's convenient for a scratch database, but production databases shouldn't be created this way, since model's tiny default sizes mean the database starts autogrowing on its very first bulk load.

questions.prompt: A server has one disk holding both the data file and the log file for a busy OLTP database. Write throughput is worse than expected. What's happening at the I/O level?
options: The log file is being cached entirely in the buffer pool, so disk placement shouldn't matter at all
The data file's random I/O breaks up the log's sequential write-ahead stream, and since no transaction commits until its log record is durably written, this slows every write transaction
SQL Server automatically detects the shared disk and throttles the data file's I/O to protect the log
Write-ahead logging only applies when data and log files are on separate disks
questions.explain: Data files see random I/O; log files see sequential write-ahead I/O. Sharing one disk means every seek for a data page interrupts the log's streaming writes, and since no transaction commits until its log record is durably written, this measurably slows every write transaction — exactly why data and log belong on separate physical disks.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: internally, a transaction log file isn't one undifferentiated stream — it's divided into Virtual Log Files, abbreviated ________, each a physically contiguous chunk that SQL Server can grow or reuse independently.
questions.explain: A log file that grew through many small, repeated autogrowth events ends up with a huge number of small VLFs — VLF fragmentation — which slows log-related operations like crash recovery, since SQL Server has to process every VLF. Sizing the log correctly upfront is the real fix.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about tempdb and file growth, per Lessons 22 and 23.
options: Microsoft's current guidance is multiple, equally-sized tempdb data files, generally one per logical core up to a maximum of 8
Instant File Initialization lets SQL Server skip zero-writing newly allocated space for both data files and the transaction log
Percentage-based FILEGROWTH compounds unpredictably — 10% of a 500 GB file is a 50 GB growth event, not a small one
Uneven tempdb data file sizes defeat the purpose of splitting them, because the proportional-fill algorithm allocates more heavily to the larger file
Instant File Initialization requires no special Windows privilege — it's on by default for every SQL Server service account
questions.explain: Microsoft's guidance is multiple, equally-sized tempdb files, one per logical core up to 8. Percentage growth genuinely compounds unpredictably on a large file. Uneven file sizes defeat multi-file tempdb entirely, since proportional fill favors the larger file. Instant File Initialization applies only to data files, never the log, which must always be zero-initialized — and it requires the 'Perform volume maintenance tasks' Windows right, not something granted by default.

questions.prompt: Match each storage concept to what it actually describes, pulling together Lessons 21-22.
right: The data file's typical access pattern — pages read and written wherever the data happens to live on disk
Every change is written to the log, in strict order, before the corresponding data page is written to the data file
A log file that grew through many small autogrowth events ends up with a huge number of small, inefficient internal chunks
Many sessions creating/dropping temp objects simultaneously contend for the same tempdb allocation pages when there are too few data files
questions.explain: Random I/O describes the data file's scattered access pattern. Sequential I/O via write-ahead logging describes the log's strictly-ordered writes. VLF fragmentation is the result of many small log autogrowth events. PAGELATCH contention is tempdb-specific blocking on allocation pages when too few data files exist for the concurrency level.

questions.prompt: What does Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) actually protect against?
options: Someone sniffing network traffic between the application and the SQL Server instance
A sysadmin querying a sensitive column and seeing plaintext they shouldn't be able to read
A SQL injection attack against a dynamically-built query string
Someone stealing the physical data/log files or a backup file and reading their raw bytes without the protecting certificate
An application authenticating with an expired or weak password
A query optimizer picking a bad execution plan due to stale statistics
questions.explain: TDE encrypts the data and log files on disk. If someone steals the physical .mdf/.ldf files or a backup file, they get unreadable bytes without the certificate protecting the database encryption key. TDE is transparent to applications and doesn't protect data in memory, in a result set, or from anyone with a legitimate login and permissions.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes exactly what Always Encrypted protects against, not TDE. TDE's threat model is a stolen disk or backup file — once connected with legitimate permissions, a sysadmin reads TDE-protected data just fine, because TDE never hides data from an authenticated, authorized session.

questions.prompt: A production database is restored onto a new instance for testing. Several application logins can connect to the instance fine but can't access the restored database, even though same-named users already exist inside it. What's almost certainly wrong?
options: The database's containment level was accidentally left at PARTIAL
The users were dropped during the restore and need to be recreated from scratch
TDE is blocking access because the certificate didn't travel with the backup
The database users are orphaned — their stored SIDs no longer match any server login on the new instance
questions.explain: A database user's SID has to match a server login's SID for the mapping to work. After a cross-instance restore, the same-named logins on the new instance typically have different SIDs, leaving the database users orphaned — connected to the instance, but unable to touch a database whose users point at logins that don't really match. sp_change_users_login or ALTER USER ... WITH LOGIN re-links them.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about GRANT, DENY, and REVOKE, per Lesson 30.
options: DENY always wins, regardless of how many GRANTs exist elsewhere, including through other role memberships
REVOKE removes a previously granted or denied permission, returning to no explicit statement either way
A user's effective permission on an object is always just whichever role they joined first
If a user belongs to five roles and even one has a DENY on an object, that user cannot access it through any of the other four roles
GRANT and DENY cannot both exist for the same principal and object at the same time under any circumstances
questions.explain: DENY overrides any GRANT from any source, which is exactly why a DENY in even one of a user's roles blocks access regardless of grants from the other roles. REVOKE simply removes a prior GRANT or DENY, returning to no explicit statement. Effective permission is the union of every role's grants minus anything denied — not simply whichever role was joined first. And a GRANT from one role alongside a DENY from another can and do coexist on the same principal and object — that's precisely the scenario DENY's override rule exists to resolve.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the built-in `sa` login should either be renamed, or — if nothing depends on it — ________, because its name is public knowledge and makes it a favorite brute-force target.
questions.explain: Real production guidance is to disable sa if nothing depends on it, or rename it and set a long random password if it must stay enabled — because its publicly known name makes it a favorite brute-force target.

questions.prompt: Match each encryption technology to the specific threat it's designed to protect against, per Lesson 31.
right: A stolen physical disk, data/log file, or backup file
A malicious or compromised DBA with sysadmin rights reading specific sensitive columns directly
Someone sniffing network traffic between the client application and the server
questions.explain: TDE protects data at rest against a stolen disk or backup file. Always Encrypted's keys never reach the SQL Server instance, so even a sysadmin sees ciphertext in specific protected columns. TLS protects data in transit, encrypting traffic between client and server over the network.

questions.prompt: An index on a 50-million-row table shows 42% fragmentation. Which operation does the standard threshold call for, and what does that operation do to the index's statistics that a lighter operation would not?
options: REBUILD — because fragmentation is above the 30% threshold, and REBUILD also refreshes the index's statistics with a full scan, as a side effect
REORGANIZE — because fragmentation is above the 30% threshold, and REORGANIZE also refreshes statistics with a full scan
REBUILD — but statistics are left completely untouched by a rebuild, same as a reorganize
No action is needed — 42% is below the threshold where any maintenance is justified
questions.explain: The industry-standard thresholds call for REBUILD above 30% fragmentation. REBUILD drops and recreates the index from scratch, fully resolving fragmentation and refreshing the index's statistics with a full scan as a side effect — REORGANIZE, the lighter 5%-30% option, does not update statistics at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: `BACKUP LOG` only works when a database is in ________ or BULK_LOGGED recovery model — SIMPLE recovery truncates the log automatically and has no log backup chain to speak of.
questions.explain: BACKUP LOG only produces a meaningful backup in FULL or BULK_LOGGED recovery, since those are the models that retain the log for backup instead of auto-truncating it the way SIMPLE recovery does.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Ola Hallengren's Maintenance Solution, per Lesson 38.
options: It's free, open-source T-SQL scripts, not a licensed product or a managed service
It performs tasks fundamentally different from ALTER INDEX, UPDATE STATISTICS, DBCC CHECKDB, and BACKUP DATABASE/LOG
It implements the same fragmentation-aware REORGANIZE-vs-REBUILD threshold logic automatically, across every targeted database, without you writing the loop yourself
In most real production environments, it's run alongside hand-built Maintenance Plans doing the exact same tasks, for redundancy
It logs detailed execution history to tables it creates, which makes failures diagnosable instead of a silent coverage gap
questions.explain: It's genuinely free and open-source, installed by running a .sql file once. It performs exactly the same real operations Lessons 33-37 already covered, not anything fundamentally different, but it applies the fragmentation-aware threshold logic automatically across every targeted database. It logs detailed execution history for diagnosability. And in most real shops it replaces hand-built Maintenance Plans entirely, rather than running alongside them for the same tasks.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 36's realistic weekly backup rotation (full on Sunday, nightly differentials, transaction log backups every 15-30 minutes), put these restore steps in the correct order to recover a database as far forward as possible.
items: Restore the most recent full backup (from Sunday)
Restore the most recent differential backup taken after that full backup
Restore every transaction log backup taken after that differential backup, in order
Bring the database online, now recovered as far forward as the backup chain allows
questions.explain: Restoring means: last full, plus the most recent differential, plus every log backup taken after that differential, in order, then bringing the database online — fewer files to apply than restoring the full plus every log backup since Sunday, which is the entire point of taking differentials.

questions.prompt: What does a SQL Server Agent proxy do?
options: Watches for a specific error number or severity level and notifies an operator when it occurs
Stores a Windows account's encrypted password so T-SQL job steps can authenticate to the Database Engine itself
Defines when a job runs — daily, weekly, or on a recurring intra-day interval
Reusable schedule definition that multiple jobs can attach to
Lets a job step run under a specific Windows identity, built from a credential, instead of running as the SQL Server Agent service account
A person or distribution list that receives email notifications from Agent
questions.explain: A proxy wraps a credential and grants it for use by specific job-step subsystems, like CmdExec, so that step runs under an explicitly scoped Windows identity instead of inheriting whatever ambient privilege the Agent service account happens to have.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B actually describes a credential, not a proxy. A credential stores the Windows identity's encrypted secret; a proxy is the separate object that wraps a credential and grants it for use by specific job-step subsystems — the proxy is what a job step actually names, not the credential directly.

questions.prompt: A job has zero rows in `msdb.dbo.sysjobhistory`, ever, since it was created. Per Lesson 44, which of these is the LEAST likely explanation?
options: The SQL Server Agent service itself is stopped
The job's schedule (or the job itself) is disabled
A CmdExec step's proxy credential lacks rights on the target resource, causing an access-denied failure
sp_add_jobserver was never called, so the job isn't targeted at any server
questions.explain: A proxy permission failure usually DOES leave a row in sysjobhistory, with a specific access-denied message, because Agent actually attempted the step before it failed. The service being stopped, a disabled schedule or job, and a job never targeted at a server all leave NO row at all, because Agent never attempted the run — which is exactly why the proxy-permission cause is the least likely explanation for a job with zero history rows ever.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in `msdb.dbo.sysjobhistory`, the `run_status` column uses 1 for Succeeded, 2 for Retry, 3 for Canceled, and ________ for Failed.
questions.explain: run_status uses 0 for Failed, 1 for Succeeded, 2 for Retry, and 3 for Canceled — the first column a DBA checks when diagnosing a job that ran but produced the wrong result.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about SQL Server Agent's object model, per Lessons 39-42.
options: A schedule is a separate, reusable object — the same schedule can be attached to more than one job
An alert and a job are tightly coupled — every alert must be tied to exactly one job
An operator has no logic of its own — it's purely a notification destination that an alert or job failure points at
Agent stores its entire configuration in msdb, the same system database that holds backup/restore history
A job cannot have more than one step
questions.explain: Schedules are reusable objects a single definition can attach to multiple jobs. Operators are pure notification destinations with no logic of their own. Agent's entire configuration — jobs, steps, schedules, alerts, operators, history — lives in msdb. Jobs and alerts, by contrast, are related but independent: most jobs never involve an alert, and most alerts aren't tied to a job. And a job can absolutely have multiple steps run in sequence.

questions.prompt: A report joins a local table against a large remote table through a linked server, filtering the remote side down to a handful of rows with a WHERE clause. Which approach is more likely to perform well, and why?
options: A four-part name — the local optimizer always pushes every predicate down to the remote side efficiently
OPENQUERY — it pushes the whole query to the remote server, so the remote optimizer can filter using its own indexes and statistics before anything crosses the network
Either approach performs identically, since both ultimately execute the same SQL text
Neither — linked server queries can't filter on the remote side at all, regardless of syntax
questions.explain: A four-part name lets the local optimizer decide how much work happens remotely, and it doesn't always push predicates down efficiently — it can pull far more rows across the network than necessary before filtering locally. OPENQUERY sends the whole query to execute entirely on the remote server using its own indexes and statistics, so only the already-filtered result crosses the network — the better choice when real filtering should happen remotely.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the SQL Server Browser service, which resolves a named instance's dynamically assigned port for connecting clients, listens on UDP port ________.
questions.explain: SQL Server Browser listens on UDP 1434 and responds with the actual port a named instance is using, since named instances typically listen on a dynamically assigned port rather than the default instance's static TCP 1433.

questions.prompt: Match each networking term to what it actually controls, per Lessons 47-48.
right: The standard protocol required for any remote client-server connection over a network
An alternative protocol mostly used for local or same-domain network connections, largely legacy today
Fastest protocol, but usable only for connections originating on the same machine as the instance
UDP 1434 service resolving a named instance's dynamic port for connecting clients
questions.explain: TCP/IP is required for any remote connection over the network. Named Pipes is a largely legacy alternative for local/same-domain connections. Shared Memory is the fastest but local-machine-only protocol. SQL Server Browser resolves a named instance's dynamic port for clients, listening on UDP 1434.

questions.prompt: A nightly job needs to know exactly what a customer's address column changed FROM and TO, for an audit log. Would SQL Server's Change Tracking feature satisfy that requirement?
options: Yes — Change Tracking stores full before/after row images for every tracked table by default
Yes, but only if the table's primary key is a single column rather than a composite key
No — neither Change Tracking nor Change Data Capture can ever capture old and new column values
No — Change Tracking only records that a row changed, by primary key and version number; it never stores the actual old and new values, which is exactly what Change Data Capture is for
questions.explain: Change Tracking answers 'which rows changed' lightweight and by key — it does not store old and new values at all. Change Data Capture is the heavier feature that reads the transaction log to capture full before/after row images, which is exactly what an audit trail needing actual historical values requires.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about deployment strategies, per Lesson 50.
options: A DACPAC-based deployment compares the package against the live target database and generates the diff script automatically
Migration-based tools like Flyway, Liquibase, or DbUp track numbered, one-directional migration scripts, with rolling back meaning writing a separate down migration
DACPAC deployment natively carries data migrations, like backfilling a new column's values
The expand-contract pattern lets a schema change like a column rename happen as one instantaneous ALTER with no staged rollout
Manual scripted deployment's real advantage is that a human reads every line before it runs, catching subtle issues like a NOT NULL column added to a table with existing rows
questions.explain: DACPAC deployment compares the package against the live database and generates the diff automatically. Migration tools track numbered, one-directional scripts where rollback means a separate down migration. DACPAC deployment is schema-only and isn't designed to carry data migrations — that logic has to be scripted separately. Expand-contract exists precisely because some changes can't happen as one instantaneous operation without risk; it's a staged pattern, not a single ALTER. And manual scripting's genuine advantage is human review catching subtle issues before they run.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the gap between what source control says a database's schema should be and what the live database actually looks like is called schema ________.
questions.explain: Schema drift happens in mundane ways — an index added live during an incident and never backported, a hotfix applied under pressure with every intention of committing it later that never comes. Detecting it regularly, via schema compare, turns it from a deployment-day surprise into something caught while it's still small.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 54, a database change goes through proper change management rather than being typed directly into a production query window. Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Write the forward migration script and its paired rollback script together, before any deployment
Have a second person review the change through a pull request
Apply the script against a restored copy of the database on a staging instance to confirm it runs clean
Deploy the change in production inside a transaction, during a scheduled low-traffic window
Verify the change took effect correctly and record it in the change log
questions.explain: The forward and rollback scripts are written together up front, then reviewed by a second person, then tested against a staging restore, then deployed transactionally during a low-traffic window, and finally verified and recorded — exactly the order that turns an ad hoc schema change into a safe, reviewed, reversible one.

questions.prompt: `sys.databases.log_reuse_wait_desc` shows `ACTIVE_TRANSACTION` for a database whose log has grown enormous overnight. Would running a log backup fix this by itself?
options: No — the log can't truncate past an open transaction no matter how often backups run; the open transaction has to be committed or rolled back first
Yes — a log backup always truncates the log regardless of what log_reuse_wait_desc reports
No — ACTIVE_TRANSACTION means log backups have never been configured for this database at all
Yes, but only if the database is first switched to SIMPLE recovery model
questions.explain: ACTIVE_TRANSACTION means an open transaction — sometimes a forgotten BEGIN TRAN with no matching commit — is preventing the log from truncating past that point, no matter how often log backups run. The fix is finding and resolving the open transaction; running another log backup by itself won't help until that happens.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about incident triage methodology, per Lesson 55.
options: The first step is confirming the reported problem is real and actually matches what's being reported, before doing anything else
The priority during the first phase of an incident is fully understanding the root cause before taking any stabilizing action
Stabilizing — like killing a runaway session — can happen before anyone knows the exact underlying cause
Communication is a separate step that only happens after the incident is fully resolved
Assessing blast radius and severity comes before diving into the technical 'why,' because it determines how urgently to act and who needs to know
questions.explain: Triage starts by confirming the problem is real, then assesses blast radius and severity before asking why, then stabilizes before fully root-causing — killing a runaway session can stabilize a server before anyone knows which query or parameter caused it. Communication runs the whole time in parallel with the technical response, not as a step reserved for after resolution.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a postmortem that treats an incident as a system failure to understand rather than a person to punish is called a ________ postmortem, per Lesson 59.
questions.explain: A blameless postmortem is only useful because people are honest in it, and people are honest when they aren't worried about being blamed — assigning blame teaches people to hide mistakes and omit details next time, the opposite of what the document is for.

questions.prompt: Match each incident-response term to what it actually means, per Lessons 57-59.
right: A written, specific reference mapping known incident symptoms to concrete diagnostic and response steps
An event that is both urgent — needs attention now — and actually actionable by whoever is currently on call
How much of the system, and how many users, an incident actually affects
A condition that worsened an incident or delayed detection, alongside the root cause
questions.explain: A runbook maps known symptoms to concrete steps. Paging-worthy means both urgent and actionable right now. Blast radius is how much of the system an incident affects, a key input to escalation decisions. A contributing factor is a condition alongside the root cause that made an incident worse or slower to detect.

questions.prompt: A team plans a major-version in-place upgrade for Friday night with 'we'll just roll it back if there's a problem' as the entire rollback plan. What will actually happen if the upgrade causes serious problems?
options: SQL Server automatically reverts the in-place upgrade if any error occurs during setup.exe
The team can simply lower the database's compatibility level to undo the upgrade

There is no supported way to downgrade a database back to the older version in place — the only real rollback is restoring a pre-upgrade backup onto a separate instance still running the old version, which doesn't exist here
A side-by-side migration is unnecessary here because in-place upgrades are always reversible
questions.explain: Once setup.exe has upgraded the system databases, there's generally no supported path to downgrade a database back to an older major version. 'Rollback' for an in-place major upgrade almost always means restoring a pre-upgrade backup onto a separately available old-version instance — and since this team never prepared that instance or a verified backup, there is effectively no real rollback plan at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: for SQL Server 2017 and later, Microsoft delivers all fixes — security, bug, and performance — through a single, fully cumulative mechanism called the ________.
questions.explain: Service Packs were phased out after SQL Server 2016. Every CU is itself cumulative — CU12 contains everything CU1 through CU11 contained plus more — so you install the latest CU for your version and you're current, with no chain of updates to install.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about upgrade and patching practice, per Lessons 60-62.
options: When an instance is upgraded in place, its databases keep their old compatibility level by default, which is a deliberate, common practice
Raising compatibility level immediately is required the moment the physical engine version changes — the two settings can never be set independently
The Data Migration Assistant (DMA) produces an assessment of deprecated features and breaking changes before an upgrade is touched
Query Store's Regressed Queries report compares old and new execution plans side by side to catch performance regressions after a test upgrade
Testing an upgrade against a database seeded with a handful of made-up rows is just as reliable as restoring a real production backup to staging
questions.explain: Databases keep their pre-upgrade compatibility level by default after an in-place upgrade, deliberately, so optimizer-behavior changes can be tested separately from the physical upgrade — compatibility level is a genuinely separate dial from the engine version, not something that must change in lockstep with it. DMA assesses deprecated features and breaking changes before anything is touched. Query Store's Regressed Queries report compares old and new plans side by side. A database seeded with a handful of made-up rows won't surface the skewed data distributions and production-scale query patterns that only show up with a real restored backup.

questions.prompt: What is a break-glass account, in the context the capstone uses the term?
options: An account that automatically escalates to sysadmin whenever a severity-16 alert fires
A dedicated, least-privilege application login used for everyday production connections
A temporary account created fresh for each maintenance window and deleted afterward
The account SQL Server Agent uses to run CmdExec steps by default
A read-only reporting account scoped to a single schema
An emergency-only admin credential, disabled day-to-day and tightly controlled, used only when normal access is unavailable
questions.explain: In the capstone, sa is kept as a break-glass account — its password rotated to a long random value stored only in a vault, and disabled day-to-day — rather than being dropped entirely, so there's still an emergency fallback if normal access is ever unavailable.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes exactly the opposite role — dispatchtrack_svc, the dedicated least-privilege login the application actually connects with every day. A break-glass account is deliberately NOT used for routine connections; sa stays disabled precisely so it's never the everyday credential, only an emergency fallback.

questions.prompt: Dispatchers across all 40 terminals can't update load statuses; updates just hang with no errors. The query above traces a blocking chain to session 82, which `sys.dm_exec_sessions` shows has `open_transaction_count = 1` and a request that finished executing eleven minutes ago. What is session 82 almost certainly doing, and what's the fix?
options: It's running a legitimate long report, and the fix is to wait for it to finish naturally rather than interrupting it
It ran an ad hoc UPDATE inside an explicit BEGIN TRANSACTION and never committed or rolled back — after trying to reach the user, ending the session with KILL releases the held locks
It's deadlocked with another session, so SQL Server will automatically choose a victim within seconds
It's a runaway CPU-bound query, and the fix is to raise its MAXDOP rather than kill it
questions.explain: open_transaction_count = 1 with a request that finished eleven minutes ago is the signature of an open, idle transaction — the session isn't actively running anything, but its row locks are still held. After trying to reach the user directly, KILLing the session rolls back the open transaction and releases the locks immediately, clearing the blocking chain.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the capstone's security and maintenance remediation (Lessons 65-66).
options: sa is kept, but disabled day-to-day, with its password rotated and stored only in a password vault
dispatchtrack_svc is added to the sysadmin fixed server role so the application never hits a permission error
The log-backup job scheduled every 15 minutes is the single change that fixes the runaway transaction log growth for good
Ola Hallengren's scripts are installed and replace the single disabled vendor job that previously existed
max server memory is left at its default because the server only has 32 GB of RAM, which is considered too little to bother capping
questions.explain: sa is kept as a break-glass account, rotated and vaulted, not dropped. The 15-minute log-backup job is exactly what fixes the runaway log growth for good, truncating it on a predictable schedule instead of letting it grow unbounded. Ola Hallengren's scripts replace the one disabled leftover vendor job. dispatchtrack_svc is scoped to db_datareader/db_datawriter plus EXECUTE, not sysadmin — the whole point was retiring the over-privileged sa-based connection. And max server memory is explicitly capped to 26,624 MB on the 32 GB box, leaving 6 GB for the OS, not left at its unlimited default.

questions.prompt: Put these five beats of the MERSQL01 capstone in the order they actually happened, per Lessons 64-68.
items: Discovery: auditing the inherited server's real configuration — sa enabled, no log backups, no maintenance jobs, no change history
Fixing the foundation: separating storage onto dedicated volumes, reconfiguring tempdb, capping max server memory
Securing and automating maintenance: retiring sa for a least-privilege login, turning on auditing, installing Ola Hallengren's scripts
Handling a production incident: finding and killing the head blocker behind a 40-terminal blocking chain
Deploying a schema change safely: a reviewed, staging-tested, transaction-wrapped migration with a rollback script prepared in advance
questions.explain: The capstone follows the order the course taught the material in: discovery first, then the foundation (architecture and storage), then security and maintenance automation, and only once that tooling exists do the incident response and change-management lessons land — exactly the sequence Lesson 64 lays out for turning a pile of problems into a prioritized plan.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: through scheduled log backups every 15 minutes, DispatchDB's Recovery Point Objective went from undefined (weeks of possible data loss) down to ________ minutes.
questions.explain: Scheduling the DatabaseBackup - USER_DATABASES - LOG job every 15 minutes gives DispatchDB a concrete 15-minute RPO, replacing an undefined exposure where the only backups were Russ's occasional, weeks-old manual fulls.
